metric_rationale: The design contains 8 unique pairs (trials 1-6, 13-14; 48 of 96 trials) where the highest-validity discriminating cue points to one option while the unweighted tally of feature-wise wins points to the other. The metric is simply the proportion of choices on these directional-conflict trials that agree with the top-cue (Take-The-Best) option. Take-The-Best predicts this proportion to be high (approximately (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, i.e. ~0.85-1.0 for most parameter draws), whereas Tallying predicts it to be low (approximately eps/2, i.e. ~0.0-0.25), since Tallying actively chooses the opposite option with a margin of 1-3 votes. The contrast is opposite in sign, so the mean gap is very large (~0.7), and because the metric is averaged over 48 trials per subject its per-subject sampling noise is tiny; the only between-subject spread comes from lapse rate, keeping variance around 0.01-0.03 for both theories. Restricting to conflict trials only (excluding tally-tie and agreement trials) maximizes the separation, and the A/B side balance of the design means no response bias can mimic either pattern.

The design contains conflict trials where the top-validity cue (or, when it ties, the 0.80 cue) favours one option while 4-5 lower-validity cues favour the other, giving tally margins of 3 or 4 (trial pairs 1/2, 5/6, 7/8, both A/B mirrorings). On exactly these trials the two heuristics make OPPOSITE-SIGN predictions, so the metric 'proportion of choices matching the tally winner' is pushed toward 1 by Tallying (a margin of 3-4 multiplied by beta saturates the softmax for almost all beta in [0.1,20]) and toward 0 by Take-The-Best (which picks the single-cue winner with probability sigmoid(beta), i.e. the tally loser). Restricting to margin>=3 keeps the Tallying-side signal near ceiling so the per-subject value is tight, and mirrored A/B versions of every pair mean no side bias can inflate or deflate the score. Each subject contributes ~36 trials to the estimate, so binomial noise is small; the remaining between-subject spread comes only from the sampled beta/epsilon, which affects both theories symmetrically around 0.5. Predicted values: Tallying ~0.8, TTB ~0.2.

Both models are compared on the SAME quantity: agreement with the Take-The-Best choice (the option favoured by the highest-validity discriminating expert). Trials are split, using the design's own structure, into (i) pairs where an absolute-evidence integrator's margin also strongly favours the TTB option (single-cue-discriminating .85 pairs, unanimous pairs, and the 1-opposing-cue conflicts) and (ii) pairs where an integrator's summed log-odds margin REVERSES the TTB choice (3-opposing, 5-opposing, and the TTB-descent pairs). Ambiguous near-zero-margin pairs are dropped. The metric is the within-subject difference in TTB-agreement between these two trial sets. Under Take-The-Best only the RANK of the first discriminating cue matters, so agreement is the same constant sigmoid(beta)-based value in both sets for every subject regardless of beta and epsilon: the difference is 0 up to binomial sampling noise (36 trials per set, sd ~0.10). Under AEWI the difference is large and positive (~0.94 vs ~0.19, i.e. ~0.75) and is insensitive to its gamma/beta ranges. Because the contrast is taken within subject, individual differences in noise/lapse cancel for TTB, giving a huge mean gap with tight per-subject variance in both theories.

Take-The-Best is rank-based and all-or-none: whatever its beta and epsilon, its choice probability for the top-discriminating-cue option is one constant number on EVERY pair where some cue discriminates. Hence any within-subject difference in TTB-consistency between two trial families must be zero for TTB, no matter how noisy or lapsy an individual subject is - this makes the contrast immune to TTB's very wide beta/epsilon ranges, which would wreck any raw accuracy/consistency measure through between-subject variance.

The two families are selected mechanically from the stimuli (no trial-index hardcoding): (a) AGREEMENT pairs where the AEWI absolute log-odds margin is large (|E| >= 1.5) and points the same way as the top discriminating cue - these are the 0.90-vs-{0.62,0.55} pairs (|E|~2.5) and the unanimous 7-0 pairs (|E|~8.5); (b) CONFLICT pairs where the margin is substantial (|E| >= 0.5) but points AGAINST the top discriminating cue - these are 0.90 vs {0.82,0.78,0.74} (|E|~1.24) and the TTB-descent pairs 0.82 vs {0.78,0.74} (|E|~0.66). Each family contains 24 trials per subject (2 mirrored pair types x 6 reps x 2 A/B orders), so binomial noise per subject is small.

Predictions: AEWI ~0.99 - ~0.15 = ~0.84 with tight per-subject variance (gamma range is narrow, both families sit far from the zero-margin crossing, which I deliberately excluded by the |E| thresholds - pairs 3-6 and 11-14 are dropped precisely because they are the high-variance ones). TTB ~0.00 with only binomial spread (<=0.02 variance). The mirrored A/B design also cancels any side bias.

The two accounts are dissociated most sharply on a subset of the designed pairs: (a) single-strong-cue trials (only the .92 expert discriminates), (b) two-weak-cue trials (.55 + .62 discriminate), (c) 2-vs-4 splits with the top cue on the small side, and (d) unanimous 6-0 dominance pairs. I select trials programmatically by simulating both models at representative parameter values and keeping only pairs where (i) the two models' predicted p(A) fall on opposite sides of 0.5 and (ii) both models are decisive there (|p-0.5| not tiny). This automatically isolates exactly those four mirrored trial families (48 of the 96 trials) and excludes the pairs where the models agree (top-cue-conflict, mid 1v1, equal-tally) or where one model sits at chance and would only inject noise.

The score is the proportion of those trials on which the subject chose the option favoured by RD-WEI (i.e. the option carrying the SMALLER compressed-weight count of positive marks). Under RD-WEI this should be ~0.85-0.92 (reversed frame, near-ceiling on lopsided normalized splits, attenuated only by lapses and the small forward-frame minority). Under AEWI it should be ~0.10-0.15, since absolute log-odds weighting makes the .92 cue and the unanimous pairs near-deterministic in the opposite direction. Because the selected trials are the ones where BOTH models are confident, per-subject variability is small on each side, so the mean gap (~0.75) should dwarf between-subject spread at N=25. Crucially the metric is not trivially true for my theory: it is a directional accuracy score defined on trial families where any forward integrator (tallying, Franklin, TTB, naive Bayes) would land near 0, so it tests the reversed-plus-normalized signature rather than restating it.

This isolates the two trial families where the two theories make maximally opposed, low-variance predictions: (a) the unanimous 7-0 dominance pairs (trials 13/14) and (b) the pairs decided by the single highly diagnostic 0.95 expert (trials 3/4). In both families I score the fraction of choices for the option carrying the POSITIVE expert ratings on the discriminating cue(s). AEWI is a forward integrator in absolute log-odds units: the margin is 4.61 (single 0.95 cue) or ~10.7 (unanimous), so choices are essentially deterministic toward the positively-rated option, giving ~0.98-1.00 with only the small lapse (eps<=0.03) pulling it down. RD-WEI's subject-level reversed polarity frame (s=-1 for ~97% of subjects) means the positively-marked option is systematically AVOIDED, and divisive normalization keeps the reversed choice confident even on the single-cue pairs, giving ~0.02-0.08. The metric therefore has a mean gap near 0.95 while being extremely tight per subject (24 trials each, near-ceiling/near-floor binomials), so it survives Welch's test at N=25. It is not trivially true for AEWI: any near-tally forward integrator would also score high, and a lexicographic TTB rule would too \u2014 the metric is diagnostic of the polarity/absolute-margin claim, not of the specific weighting exponent.
